quote: The unshowy dedication to craft is a marvel, and so is much else in this crystalline little film. It’s the most exhilarating experience I’ve had at the movies this year.
Johnson shapes this material with both breeziness and a kind of tough-love compassion, and the track list he’s assembled summons the spirit of 1975 like a ghost.
Kudos to Johnson, though, for not going full Hollywood with his first Hollywood cast. He’s still fascinated by lively rebels, and, with Anthony Bourdain, he found the perfect subject.

Tony equates ambition and intellectual curiosity with a desire to taste, experience, and understand everything life has to offer, which is wildly entertaining and, quite literally, a thoughtful chef’s kiss.
This coming of age story does not hew to the contours of biography. It instead opts for a familiar arc that uses its tropes as an asset, not a distraction.
The tart yet tender comedy provides some insight for Bourdain fans to connect the dots. But you don’t need to be familiar with his life and career to appreciate this crowd-pleasing origin story.

Memories of Bourdain as a public figure are not included in Matt Johnson’s evocative and often hilarious coming-of-age story, but they’re like the hidden ingredient that enhances and completes a dish.
Even in its cheesiest moments, Tony remains grounded, thanks to its earthy performances and warm, sun-dappled visual style.

Johnson has given us the prequel to a life. This is Anthony Bourdain choosing life and the world, finding his place in it through hard lessons, wild times, and good people he learned from in those early days.
The story is slight, but by concentrating on this crucial sliver of a teeming life, Johnson gets at something deeper and more universal than a wider focus might have allowed.
The combo of Johnson’s need to turn an individual’s tale into something doggedly universal, with a purposeful lack of affection for the subject, makes you wonder why they bothered making it.

An uneasy yet riveting watch. In this fictionalized exploration of young Anthony Bourdain, Dominic Sessa captures the exhausting, irascible, unlikable narcissist personality of the late acclaimed chef and TV personality.
A Hollywood Bildungsroman of the finest old-fashioned sort...a movie set in the mid-1970s that actually feels as though it might have been made then, which, it turns out, is a good thing.
Tony is worth seeing in the end, I suppose, but as cinematic meals go, it is one that still leaves you feeling a little hungry when it is all over.
Tony ... probably would have been just as compelling if it had been about some random or fictional guy instead of a famous one.

The kitchen scenes are a combo platter of boot camp, frat house hazing ritual and kung fu movie. As Bourdain would later explain, he thrived in a setting where actions have instant consequences: a sore back, a sliced hand, a good meal.
Tony is a delightfully charming and bittersweet portrait of someone whose life would eventually become larger than he ever imagined.
Some of the dramatic license Johnson takes bothered me, but I went along for the ride. I appreciated the movie’s willingness to spice up the coming-of-age formula.
Tony thrives on how well the renowned television figure is depicted by Sessa, and how the story is told in such a warm and appealing way despite Bourdain’s rougher edges.
Matt Johnson’s compelling, visually scrumptious and superbly acted picture is a thoughtful coming-of-age drama that just happens to be a "prequel origin story" focused on Anthony Bourdain.

Johnson ups his game with "Tony," smoothly transitioning into more serious filmmaking, but he hasn’t lost his spirit, and his version of the Bourdain experience certainly helps to understand the subject in a new light.
Though the kitchen scenes in Tony are the only fun ones ... the film doesn't do a particularly great job of selling you on the idea that this version of Bourdain actually loved food, which he did.
Tony works as both a fond tribute and a sharp coming-of-age drama.
Thankfully, the performances are as finely honed as the script. As young Bourdain, Sessa embodies the future food star in his physicality.
As a biopic, Tony takes a low-key but still-compelling approach to one summer in the life of 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain. The cast, led by a magnetic Dominic Sessa as Bourdain, is top-notch.
Focusing on a slice of time from a cultural icon is a now-savvy alternative to the cradle-to-grave biopic. But “Tony” fails as an origin story. The cook is off.
I admired Tony the movie even if I found it very difficult to root for Tony the human being.
Tony is a terrific film. One that should be remembered for ages to come
A captivating, heartfelt and funny coming-of-age drama. Dominic Sessa gives a warm, tender and Oscar-worthy performance.

If you admire Anthony Bourdain’s boisterous way of getting you to take "just one bite," or if his sentimentality caused you to be more vulnerable with strangers, it would be best to keep your Bourdain fantasies intact and skip watching this abstraction.
Sessa is up to the task of finding both the deep uncertainty and brash confidence in this complex young man, sometimes in the same beat.

While Tony does have its moments of chaos and tension, Johnson delivers a remarkably warm and tender film that feels very fresh and singular while never sacrificing any of Johnson’s more notable formal quirks.
Tony is a coming-of-age story that anyone can connect with.

A typical coming-of-age film tends to prioritize the product over the process of transformation. "Tony," however, allows the audience to luxuriate in the people and places that its subject loved best.

At its lovable best, “Tony” fondly reminds us of the man who could never shoot a successful fishing segment, went on head-pounding benders in Greece and helped teach the world that food could change lives.
Proof that you don’t need to change a great old recipe to deliver a delicious dish.

Bourdain devotees will likely enjoy seeing the early years of the chef brought to life, though it's hard to root for a self-described "spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout" as a character.
Tony is simply a terrifically composed coming-of-age story told with warmth, attention to detail, and emotional depth.
Tony is one of the best kinds of summer movies – one where you want to live in this world for as long as you feel like it.
A film that works as a successful distillation of what Bourdain was about, while also telling a self-contained story that doesn’t require any knowledge of Bourdain’s life in order to appreciate it.

Matt Johnson's biopics don’t feel like traditional biopics. No, they are stories that happen to be about real people while homing in on relatable circumstances without sacrificing his tremendous Nirvanna comedic sensibilities. Tony Is no exception
It's crass, it's loud, it's messy, and yet, you end up with something profound, beautiful, and exciting on your plate.
As with "BlackBerry," Johnson brings a winning, warts-and-all texture to the film, making it a recognizable yet tasty dish.
Beyond its dutiful biopic services, Tony reminds its audience of the sharp turns and unlikely encounters that can change the course of our lives and give us stories to share over the dinner table.

Sessa's take on the nineteen year-old Bourdain is of an angry young man with a chip on his shoulder, someone overly confident in his abilities needing to be knocked down a few pegs, yet with an undeniable, surly charm...

A hangout movie is perhaps the most fitting way for Bourdain to be brought to the screen. Though its ambitions never quite match its subject, it depicts a summer you’ll be hard-pressed not to be charmed by.
Even if Tony were not a biopic at all, but simply the fictional story of one screwed-up kid’s transformative summer working in a restaurant kitchen, it would be a movie worth watching.
The best that can be said about Tony is that the movie never takes itself too seriously and is entertaining from beginning to end.
It eschews the conventional biopic formula, but in doing so seems to amble aimlessly, much like its central character, in search of something to do.

Tony doesn’t give Tony too much growth by the end, but it does highlight some core values that Bourdain would express in his work as an adult: The pleasure of creation, the beauty of consumption, and the power of the unassuming and unexpected.

Few biopics these days truly present their subjects warts and all. In life, it seemed Bourdain was secure enough to own his mistakes, and presenting them unflinchingly makes Tony's story far more resonant.
As a film about what it means to embrace what’s in front of you and not what’s in your mind, it’s a lovely and deeply likeable work.
To me, if an Anthony Bourdain biopic can’t clear the bar called “Bourdain would have liked it,” it’s probably not a good movie. “Tony” clears that bar.
Fresh, intoxicating, profound and deeply resonant, this heartfelt dramedy is a must-see.

A slender slice of a famous life, the movie feels a little wispy in its mix of scrappy and sweet, rough-edged and yet bathed in the balming glow of nostalgia. But it has an idiosyncratic charm that fits the title character.
“Tony” struggles for an ending, but it doesn’t really need one; the real fun here lies in paving the way to parts unknown.
With Banderas particularly touching as Bourdain’s unlikely father figure, Tony immerses us in this sleepy Massachusetts community and the character’s gradual artistic awakening.
Whether you are a fan of Anthony Bourdain, someone who loves chef-centric media like The Bear, or are just looking for a funny, inspiring story, Tony offers something for everyone.
This is a strange film in some ways. It is watchable and entertaining, but its feelgood trajectory is compromised by what we know of the author.

It might focus on the origins of a beloved pop-culture figure, but there are so many moments in which you can forget about the beats and markers of Bourdain’s real life and simply enjoy it as a story about one man’s voracious aspirations and appetites.
The bond between the two is phenomenal -- Banderas' performance is tender, powerful, and an unexpected standout in the film.
If nothing else, it’s a welcome sign that Johnson can retain his signature voice while dropping some elements of his style and finding interest in a topic he might not care all that much about.
'Tony' does earn our affection, mostly because it never pretends Bourdain has. We are invited to view the genius as a work in progress.

A zesty, energetic biopic about a teenage Anthony Bourdain, Matt Johnson’s second film this year is an act of controlled chaos, tapping into the nostalgia of naïve youth while examining how creativity is born.
At a time when so many biopics feel like formulaic compilations of a person’s greatest hits or cinematic renderings of their Wikipedia summary, Matt Johnson’s Tony feels like a breath of fresh air.
Sessa once again employs an infectious charm that complements the inner turmoil of a young man navigating his own identity crisis. It’s a wonderfully endearing turn by a promising young actor.
Has a rough-around-the-edges charm that’s in keeping with its go-for-broke protagonist.

Matt Johnson... has once again taken true-story source material and made a real movie. It works on its own terms, with or without the halo of its subject's career. It's actually about something. And it's a delight to watch.
Tony is a captivating look at a formative summer in the life of Anthony Bourdain.

It unflinchingly probes into the mayhem of Anthony’s adolescence, complete with compulsive lying and reckless shenanigans. Dominic Sessa fully commits to the role but it’s Antonio Banderas who delivers the most beautifully understated performance.
The film is more interested in the passions that kept Anthony Boudrain's demons at bay than in how those demons ultimately consumed him.
